place.zh: 石坳村 · 屋后柴垛 · 半夜

setup.zh: 日头偏西，你去村东头背回那只缸，吴婆婆讲了一个很短的故事：一口鼎，一条龙，一张掉下来的弓——鼎湖，乌号。半夜里，柴垛上，它睁开了一只眼睛。你问她：真的有仙人？
setup.en: Toward evening you fetch the crock back from the east end, and Granny Wu tells a very short story: a *ding*, a dragon, a bow that fell — Dinghu, Wuhao. At midnight on the woodpile it opens one eye. You ask her: are there really immortals?

recap.zh: 吴婆婆讲了鼎湖：上去的上去了，留下的，就守着一张弓。银月醒了一回：仙人是真的，凡人能修。次夜她留下洗髓丹、《吐纳经》和一个「藏」字，钻进了木牌；那声谢谢，她没听见。
recap.en: Granny Wu told of Dinghu: those who went up went up; those left behind kept a bow. Yinyue woke once: immortals are real, mortals can cultivate. The next night she left a Marrow-Washing Pill, *The Classic of Breathing* and one word — hide — and went into the token; the thank-you, she never heard.

zh: 柴垛上，一团凉冰冰的银毛。
断口渗出的血，是银的，像落了一层霜。
半夜，它睁开了一只眼睛。
en: On the woodpile, a cold curl of silver fur.
The blood from its cuts is silver, like a fall of frost.
At midnight, it opens one eye.

story.zh:
日头偏西，他娘叫他去村东头把缸背回来。吴婆婆的脸已经朝着西边了，听见缸响，道：「弓，回来了？」小满道：「回来了。」她便仰着脸，讲了一个很短的故事。

早年间，天底下头一个皇帝，在一座山底下铸了一口鼎。鼎成那天，天上下来一条龙接他，皇帝骑上去，大官、娘娘跟着爬上去七十几个。剩下一个小官儿挤不上去，扑上去抓住了龙须，吊在半空里；他有个闺女，才七八岁，在底下仰着脸，一声一声地喊爹。龙须扯断了，人都掉了下来，跟着掉下来的，还有那皇帝的一张弓。后来的人，管那地方叫鼎湖，管那张弓，叫乌号。她讲到那闺女仰着脸喊爹，自己的脸也仰着，朝着天上。

小满道：「那闺女呢？」吴婆婆道：「……哭呗。」又道：「上去的上去了，留下的，就守着一张弓。」小满问道：「那张弓，后来有人拉开过吗？」吴婆婆转过脸来，朝着他，慢慢地露出一个笑来：「你问得好。」便不再往下说了，只自言自语地添了一句：「修仙修仙，修成个想上天的人，也就修到头了。」

那天夜里，小满把「围脖」抱到了屋后的柴垛上。柴垛上没人，只有月亮。

它一整天都没醒。身子还是凉的，尾根上那八道断口又渗出血来，银色的，一滴一滴落在柴草上，像下了一层霜。他把它捧在膝盖上，拿身子挡着风。半夜里，它睁开了一只眼睛，头一句便是：「……吵死了。你喘气那么大声干什么。」

小满长长地松了一口气，差点哭出来。有一个问题，他憋了一整天：「吴婆婆讲过，蒙山顶上住过一个骑白鹤的老头，活了八百岁。我爹说那是编的。仙人，真有？」

「你爹说错了。」银月道，「仙人，是真的。本王见过的仙人，比你见过的鸡还多。」她哼了一声，「他们从前也都是凡人，跟你一样，饿了就啃饼。后来学会了把天地间的灵气，一点一点收进自己的身子里，像你娘往缸里存米。存够了，不老，不病，力能搬山。——就这么点事，叫修仙。」

柴垛上很静。隔了好一会儿，小满才问：「骑龙的……是像吴婆婆讲的那个皇帝那样？」银月的耳朵，动了一下。她看着月亮，看了很久，久到小满以为她又睡着了，才道：「……本王不记得了。」她说的是「不记得」，不是「不知道」。小满当时没听出这两样有什么分别。

「那……我也能？」「能。但很难。一百个，九十九个老死了事。」「灵气是什么？经脉是什么？」「问他们。这世上有一群人，专门教人修仙。比本王有耐心。……当然，没本王教得好。」她的声音越来越轻，轻到后来，便没有了。她睡着了，尾巴尖儿搭在他手腕上，搭在他娘打的那个方方正正的结上。
story.en:
Toward evening his mother sent him to the east end to fetch the crock back. Granny Wu's face had turned west by now. Hearing the crock, she said, "The bow — it's back?" Xiaoman said, "It's back." So she lifted her face and told a story, a very short one.

Long ago, the very first emperor under heaven cast a *ding* at a mountain's foot. The day it was cast, a dragon came down from the sky to fetch him; the emperor climbed on, and his great officers and consorts climbed up after him, seventy-odd of them. One small official couldn't squeeze on; he threw himself at the dragon's whiskers and clung there, hanging in mid-air; he had a daughter, seven or eight years old, who stood below with her face turned up, calling "Father!" again and again. The whiskers tore; the people all fell; and down with them fell the emperor's bow. Later people called that place Dinghu, and that bow, Wuhao. When she came to the daughter calling her father with her face turned up, her own face was turned up too, toward the sky.

Xiaoman said, "And the daughter?" Granny Wu said, "…Cried, what else." She paused, then went on: "Those who went up went up; those left behind kept a bow." Xiaoman asked: "That bow — did anyone ever draw it after?" Granny Wu turned her face to him, and slowly a smile came. "You ask well." She went no further, only added, half to herself: "Cultivating immortality, cultivating immortality — if what you've cultivated is a man who wants to go up to heaven, that's as far as it goes."

That night Xiaoman carried the "scarf" out to the woodpile behind the house. On the woodpile there was nobody, only the moon.

It hadn't woken all day. Its body was still cold, and the eight cuts at the root of its tail had begun to bleed again — silver, drop by drop onto the straw, like a fall of frost. He held it on his knees, his body between it and the wind. At midnight it opened one eye, and the first thing it said was: "…So noisy. Why do you breathe so loud?"

Xiaoman let out a long breath and nearly cried. There was a question he had been holding in all day: "Granny Wu told me an old man riding a white crane lived on top of Mount Meng once, and lived eight hundred years. Dad says that's made up. Immortals — are they real?"

"Your father's wrong," said Yinyue. "Immortals are real. This king has seen more immortals than you've seen chickens." She sniffed. "They were all mortals once, just like you — hungry, they gnawed flatbread. Then they learned to take the qi of heaven and earth into their own bodies, a little at a time, the way your mother stores rice in the jar. Store enough, and they don't age, they don't sicken, they can move mountains. — That's all it is. They call it cultivating immortality."

The woodpile was very quiet. A good while later Xiaoman asked, "The ones who ride dragons… like the emperor in Granny Wu's story?" Yinyue's ear twitched. She looked at the moon a long time — so long Xiaoman thought she'd fallen asleep again — and said: "…This king doesn't remember." She said "doesn't remember", not "doesn't know". At the time Xiaoman didn't hear the difference.

"Then… could I?" "You could. It's hard. Of a hundred, ninety-nine just grow old and die." "What's qi? What are meridians?" "Ask them. There are people in this world who teach others to cultivate. More patient than this king." She paused. "…Not as good a teacher, of course." Her voice grew fainter and fainter, until it was gone. She was asleep, the tip of her tail resting on his wrist, on the square, neat knot his mother had tied.

story.zh:
第二天，她没有醒。小满隔一会儿便低头看一眼胸口，他娘问他胸口疼？他说不疼，看看还在不在。

到了夜里，是银月把他叫醒的。小满睡在柴垛上——他跟他娘说屋里挤，他娘看了他一眼，给了他一床破棉絮——睡到半夜，只觉得胸口一凉，像揣着的一块冰忽然化开了。他一激灵坐了起来，那团银毛已经从他怀里钻了出来，蹲在柴垛顶上，对着月亮。

她的样子，比昨天更差了。银色的血是不渗了，可整个身子薄得像一层纸，月光能从她身上透将过去。薄一分，又薄一分——她在谷里说的，原来是这个样子。她道：「听着。本王要睡一阵子。」「多久？」「不知道。伤太重，得闭关。」她看着他，「在本王醒过来之前，你得自己走。」

她从颈子底下一只旧得发黑的小布袋里，一样一样往外吐东西。头一样是一颗药丸，黑乎乎的，鸽子蛋那么大，像烂菜叶子泡了三天的味儿。她道：「洗髓丹。今夜就泡。疼也别喊出声。」小满捏着鼻子道：「洗……洗什么？」「洗你那一身脉。」她喘了一口气，像背一句背了几千年的老话：「凡人有此八脉，俱属阴神，闭而不开。」小满道：「八脉是什么？」「你身子里八条水渠，都堵着。」「那堵着的，怎么开？」她没有答，眼皮往下一垂，接着往外吐。

第二样是一卷竹简，绳子都快烂了，竹片上还有虫蛀的眼儿。可它一落在柴草上，四下里的夜气便清了一清，像下过一场小雨；小满拿在手里，竹片竟是温的。她道：「《吐纳经》。最粗浅的入门功夫，仙界三岁的狐狸崽子都会。看不懂，也要背。」然后她看着他，一个字一个字地说道：「**藏。**」小满道：「藏什么？」

「藏本王，藏你自己。」她道，「在你打得过所有人之前，不许让任何人知道本王，不许让任何人知道你在修炼。能装傻就装傻，能示弱就示弱。——你那个吃饼的鬼，就很好。往后，你就是那个见了鬼吓得打摆子的傻孩子。」「我娘也不能说？」银月道：「你娘，用不着你说。」

小满想起他娘理围脖的那只手，想起她那句「这条围脖，挺暖和的吧」，便不再问了。「那什么时候能不藏？」「等你把欺负过你的人，一个一个，都踩在脚底下的时候。」

她的眼皮越来越沉，声音也越来越低：「还有……本王在找一个地方……一个名字……」她皱着眉，很用力地想，「……想不起来了。等你……听见了，本王会知道的……」小满道：「什么地方？什么名字？你说个大概，我替你留心——」她却已经不说了。她的身子在月光里一点一点地淡下去，淡得像灶膛里最后那一缕青烟。

小满急了。这一回，她是真的要走了，要到一个他够不着的地方去。那个字，这时候再不说，便真的来不及了。他张开嘴。「银月——」她看着他。她已经淡得快看不见了，只剩一双金色的眼睛，还在月光里亮着，等着他往下说。

他张着嘴，那个字就在舌头尖上。可不知怎的，话一出口，却变成了：「……你还欠我一张饼呢。」那双金色的眼睛，眨了一下。她的身子化成了一缕银光。那缕光绕着他转了一圈，轻轻擦过他的脸，凉凉的，钻进了他怀里，钻进了吴婆婆给他的那块狐纹木牌。木牌上那只蜷着的小狐狸，九条尾巴里，有一条亮了，银的，一明，一暗，像在很慢、很慢地呼吸。小满低头看着那块木牌，小声道：「……喂。」木牌没有回答。他又道：「你还欠我一张饼呢。」木牌，暖了一下。

他在柴垛上坐了很久，把木牌捧起来，凑到嘴边，很小很小声地说道：「银月。」停了一停。

「谢谢。」

木牌凉凉的，没有暖。那条银色的尾巴，照旧一明，一暗。它睡得太沉了，听不见。
story.en:
The next day, she didn't wake. Every little while Xiaoman looked down at his chest. His mother asked if his chest hurt; he said no, he was just checking it was still there.

At night, it was Yinyue who woke him. Xiaoman was sleeping on the woodpile — he'd told his mother the house was crowded; she'd given him a look and a ragged quilt — and in the middle of the night he felt his chest go cold, as if the lump of ice he carried had suddenly melted. He sat bolt upright; the bundle of silver fur had already crept out of his jacket and sat on top of the woodpile, facing the moon.

She looked worse than the day before. The silver blood had stopped seeping, but her whole body was as thin as paper; moonlight passed right through her. A little thinner, and a little thinner again — so this was what she had meant in the valley. She said: "Listen. This king has to sleep a while." "How long?" "Don't know. The wound's too deep; this king must go into seclusion." She looked at him. "Until this king wakes, you have to walk on your own."

From a little cloth pouch under her chin, old and blackened, she brought things out, one by one. The first was a pill, black, big as a pigeon's egg, smelling like rotten cabbage leaves soaked three days. She said: "Marrow-Washing Pill. Soak in it tonight. It hurts; don't cry out." Xiaoman pinched his nose. "Wash… wash what?" "Those channels of yours." She drew a breath, like reciting a saying some thousands of years old: "All mortals have these Eight Vessels; all belong to the yin spirit, shut and never open." Xiaoman said, "What are the Eight Vessels?" "Eight channels in your body, like ditches, all blocked." "And the blocked ones — how do they open?" She didn't answer. Her eyelids drooped, and she went on bringing things out.

The second was a bamboo scroll, its cords nearly rotted through, worm holes in the slips. Yet the moment it touched the straw, the night air around them cleared a little, as after a light rain; in Xiaoman's hands the slips were warm. She said: "*The Classic of Breathing.* The simplest beginner's skill; every three-year-old fox cub in the Immortal Realm knows it. If you can't understand it, memorise it anyway." Then she looked at him and said, word by word: "**Hide.**" Xiaoman said, "Hide what?"

"Hide this king, hide yourself," she said. "Until you can beat everyone, no one may know about this king; no one may know you are cultivating. Play the fool where you can; play the weakling where you can. — That flatbread-eating ghost of yours is exactly right. From now on you are the silly boy who saw a ghost and shook with fright." "Not even my mum?" Yinyue paused. "Your mother — you won't need to tell."

Xiaoman remembered his mother's hand straightening the scarf, remembered her "nice and warm, is it", and asked no more. "Then when can I stop hiding?" "When everyone who ever bullied you is under your feet, one by one."

Her eyelids grew heavier and heavier, her voice lower and lower: "And… this king is looking for a place… a name…" She frowned, thinking very hard. "…Can't remember. When you… hear it, this king will know…" Xiaoman said, "What place? What name? Tell me roughly and I'll keep an ear out —" But she'd stopped speaking. In the moonlight her body faded, bit by bit, thin as the last wisp of blue smoke from the stove.

Xiaoman panicked. This time she was really going, to somewhere he couldn't reach. That word — if he didn't say it now, it would truly be too late. He opened his mouth. "Yinyue —" She looked at him. She'd faded almost past seeing; only a pair of golden eyes still shone in the moonlight, waiting for him to go on.

His mouth open, the word right on the tip of his tongue. But somehow what came out was: "…You still owe me a flatbread." The golden eyes blinked once. Her body turned into a thread of silver light. The light circled him once, brushed his face, cool, slipped inside his jacket, into the fox-carved token Granny Wu had given him. Of the nine tails of the little curled fox on the token, one lit up — silver — bright, dim, as if breathing, very, very slowly. Xiaoman looked down at the token and said softly: "…Hey." The token didn't answer. He said again: "You still owe me a flatbread." The token warmed, once.

He sat on the woodpile a long time, then lifted the token to his lips and said, very, very softly: "Yinyue." A pause.

"Thank you."

The token made no sign. She was sleeping too deep. She couldn't hear.
